utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We will now move to the pre-Defence conference to be held under Rule 73 ter. Now, we have a list of issues which I discussed, of course, with the Trial Chamber. We will go through these various issues, but if I have skipped or forgotten any matter, please tell me. First of all, the date of opening of the Defence case. We have already agreed that this will be the 30th of November, and we will be sitting for three weeks until the 18th of December except probably for the 3rd and 4th of December because we have a Plenary Session of the Tribunal. If we can sit at part of those days, we will let you know. We may be needed for the Plenary Session, so it is likely that we will not be sitting on the 3rd and 4th of December. Then when we resume in January, probably on the 11th of January, until we come to the end of the Defence case. However, we will take a few days off on the 18th through the 21st of February -- sorry, first of all, the 29th of January through the 1st of February, then 18th of February through the 21st of February, and we may have to skip one or two days in January because Judge Mumba and I are likely to sit on Tadic for three or four days in January. But we will let you know in November, as soon as we start with the Defence case. At that stage, I hope that we know when we are sitting on Tadic in January. Now, as for the timetable, we want to stick to our present schedule, 9.30 to 12.30, 2.00 to 5.00 in the afternoon; however, we think we should take the Wednesday afternoon off as well as the Friday afternoon off. Otherwise, the pace is too -- I mean, it's really exhausting both for the parties and the Tribunal. So two afternoons off, Wednesday and Friday. So much for the calendar. We will come back to some more precise data when we reconvene on the 30th of November. What is now more important is to set the deadlines for Defence filings. As you know, that in 73, Rule 73 ter (B), there's a list of requirements. Now, we would like to ask the Defence to file by the 13th of November a few things, and in some cases, when these filings are for the Trial Chamber, we can wait until the 20th of November. So we would like to say that probably the Defence should turn over to the Prosecution some particular documents or exhibits or witness statements two weeks before the beginning of the Defence case whereas, if need be, we can wait until one week before the beginning of the Defence case. But I think the Prosecution needs at least two weeks before the commencement of the Defence case. Now, this applies, first of all, to admissions concerning matters that are not in dispute. We very much urge the Defence to file those admissions so that we can narrow down the matters which are in dispute. It's very important. Admissions as to facts or legal points that are not in dispute. Secondly, a statement of contested matters. If you wish, you can have just one document or two separate documents: one concerning matters that are not in dispute, another concerning matters that are indeed in dispute. Thirdly, the Defence should submit a general brief -- actually, each Defence counsel is called upon to submit a general brief setting out the main points of his or her defence, the main points. So outlining the defence for each particular accused. Number 4. We also need a list of witnesses for each accused, including witnesses for any possible sentencing. You know that under our new rules, the parties are requested to submit, and I quote from Rule 85(A)(vi) "any relevant information that may assist the Trial Chamber in determining an appropriate sentence if, if the accused is found guilty on one or more of the charges in the indictment." We now have, as you know, under our new Rules of Procedure, we have combined the two phases which previously were separate, distinct. So the Defence may wish to take into account this request to call witnesses for sentencing. List of exhibits. Again, they should be served, as all the other documents, on the Prosecution by the 13th of November. As for the Trial Chamber, we can wait until the 20th of November. It is for the Defence to decide. You may find it easier and more convenient or expedient for you to simultaneously serve those documents on the Prosecution and file them for the Trial Chamber. Now, these documents should be submitted in English. All right. So we would also like to know -- this maybe we can know today -- roughly how many witnesses will be called by each Defence counsel. I understand from Counsel Pavkovic that roughly 80, roughly speaking, 80 witnesses will be called by the various Defence counsel, but it would be interesting for us to have a rough idea of how many witnesses per counsel or per indictee will be called. By the way, the exhibits which I just mentioned a minute ago should be, of course, provided in their original form with a translation into English. We have also discussed the question of examination of witnesses. I know that Counsel Radovic said one or two days ago that he intends to call some witnesses together with Counsel Slokovic-Glumac. We would prefer to have a list of witnesses per indictee or per counsel so that we know which witnesses are called by, say, Counsel Radovic, then Counsel Slokovic-Glumac, and so on. Of course, each counsel may be interested in examining a witness called by another counsel, and you will be allowed to do so, of course if the witness called by the other counsel is relevant to your own client. We suggest the following order: First of all, examination-in-chief by the Defence counsel calling the witness; then cross-examination, if any, by the other Defence counsel; then, number 3, cross-examination by the Prosecutor; and then, 4, re-examination by the Defence counsel calling the witness but only by the Defence counsel who has called the witness. Yes, Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Glumac and myself are in a specific situation. I say this because you have now announced the rules that cross-examination is -- only the counsel who has called the witness has the right to it. A number of witnesses, since they are brothers and some of their relationships are the same and their histories are the same and many facts are the same of their lives, so we can't avoid, Mrs. Slokovic-Glumac and myself, have the same witness. We can't avoid it. And we ask the Court for us to share the witness, to have the same witness, to offer the same witness at the same time. Then there is no need for Mrs. Slokovic-Glumac to do the cross-examination herself. And that the same witness be called by me and by her. It is best to process this witness at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I would just like to add, we have the identical defence on all the counts. The accused, since the emphasis is on the 16th, they were together all that time. So taking this into account, we have the same defence and the same situations, and therefore we believe that -- I believe that we could share the witnesses. In view of their movements, all the witnesses for the 16th are the same; they didn't separate on that day at all. They were together all the time. And our defence is identical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. I will consult with my colleagues. My feeling is that you may call the same witnesses but only one of you then will be entitled to re-examine the witness after the cross-examination by your colleague, cross-examination by the Prosecutor, and then only one of you will re-examine the witness. Yes. We rule that you will be allowed to present just one common list of witnesses, and so one of you may then examine in chief the witness, the other one may cross-examine the witness. Then we will have cross-examination by the Prosecution, then only one of you may re-examine the same witness. All right. Whereas for the other Defence counsel, we will apply the rules I announced before; namely, Counsel Pavkovic, for example, decides to call 20 witnesses. He will examine in chief his witnesses, but another counsel may feel that he has to cross-examine one of those witnesses. Then the Prosecution will cross-examine the witness and then only Counsel Pavkovic will be allowed to re-examine that particular witness. All right? I very much insist that you should please comply with Rule 94 bis concerning expert witnesses so that if you comply with that Rule and you present in advance all the relevant documents to the Prosecution and we can avoid calling the expert witnesses, really, we save a lot of time. This is Rule 94 bis. So remember, 14 days. All right. So you know those rules. As for the merits. I also want -- going back to the, what I called before "legal brief," I wonder whether you could, for the sake of narrowing down the issues, the legal and factual issues in dispute, first of all address, in your legal brief, the question of persecution, the legal notion of persecution, as well as the legal issue of accumulation of charges. This will be in response to the Prosecution's brief which, as you will remember, addressed both issues. Notion of persecution -- they also took the opportunity to discuss whether or not culmination of charges is admissible before our Tribunal. There is also one particular matter which needs to be clarified. We would like to know from you whether you dispute that on the 16th of April, 1993, a massacre was carried out in Ahmici. Now, regardless of whether or not the accused were involved -- this is a different matter -- but the basic issue, because if this issue is not in dispute, of course, this would facilitate the task of the Tribunal. We would like simply to know from you what you dispute about the objective facts happening in Ahmici on the 16th of April, '93. I have gone through my notes. I wonder now whether there are matters which I neglected, whether either the Defence or the Prosecution would like to raise any matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just one point. As far as dates are concerned, the dates you mentioned earlier, if I understood well, under the 13th of April, the document number 125 should be handed to the Prosecution -- I'm sorry, I'm sorry, the 13th of November, yes. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: By the 13th of November, these documents will be handed to the Prosecution by the Defence, and on the 20th of November to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. This gives the Defence four weeks, so you would have four weeks to file admissions concerning matters that are not in dispute, (1); (2) statement of any contested matters of all the various contested matters, actually; (3) the general brief outlining the defence for each Defence counsel; (4) the list of witnesses; and (5) the list of exhibits. All this by the 13th of November. Now, as you know in Rule 73 ter, it is provided that the Defence may be requested by the Trial Chamber to submit a summary of the facts on which each witness will testify, but you may wish to submit the actual statement. It's for you. You may submit a summary, but also to be fair to the Prosecution because the Prosecution submitted not a summary but the actual statements of all the witnesses they then called, so I would urge you also to submit -- but you are not bound to do so because under Rule 73 ter, you are only bound to submit a summary of the facts. But then if it is a summary, it should be fairly accurate, not a three-line summary, because again, we must be fair to the Prosecution. They must be in a position to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Regarding this point, Mr. President, we would like that the summary of the witness statements, or the witness statements themselves, include the identity of the witness, the date of birth, and the name of the witness's father, which is very important for us so that we can check the identity of the witnesses. I would also like for you to confirm that the date of the 13th of November is the date on which we have to receive these documents and not the date on which these documents will have to be sent from Zagreb, for instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. This is a Friday. So by noon, for instance, the documents will have to be at the Tribunal, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: We acknowledge that this is the date by which the Prosecution must receive it. We will ask the Registrar to allow us travel expenses to come to The Hague because we don't trust the post office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We insist also on the order of the witnesses, so we will start with the witnesses called by Counsel Radovic and Slokovic-Glumac, then we go through all those witnesses and then start with the following -- the witnesses to be called by counsel for Vlatko Kupreskic. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Relating to the order of witnesses. We will have some problems here. Concerning the notion of persecution and the facts that we have to state starting from the general conditions in the Vitez municipality, the Vitez Brigade, the problems that existed earlier in that area, we'll try to give a rounded picture of the events at that time in that area. It will be a bit problematic because the general witnesses will be presented by myself, they will be called by myself and my colleague, for all the other counsels. Do we have to make such an order because the Prosecution did it too? He went first through the facts and the witnesses related to persecution. Could we do the same thing? We will go through the same -- through the witnesses for persecution relating to all the facts that we want to prove relating to that act, and then we will go to the individual guilt and counts for the accused. This will make matters easier for us and make our description of the situation easier. The Prosecution used the same method. They didn't use the first accused, the second accused, but then he took the list of witnesses for the notion of persecution, for instance, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: That means that you would call witnesses on Count 1, persecution, first of all, and then on the various counts concerning your clients, but on behalf of all of the Defence counsel, so then afterwards, we would not start with other witnesses on persecution called by other --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That's right, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We feel it would be more economical if you could start with Count 1, persecution. You call witnesses on Count 1 but, legally speaking, also the other counsel are entitled later on to call witnesses on Count 1 before calling witnesses on counts relating to their own clients. However, if you could deal with all those witnesses on Count 1, it would be by far more economical for the Defence case. Of course, this is an agreement which must be reached by the various Defence counsel because, in a way, you would be speaking on behalf of everybody on Count 1. You see? You have a right -- I mean, the other legal counsel have a right to call witnesses also on Count 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I thought, when I proposed this, that we include all the other counsel in that part, that we present evidence concerning Count 1, and our other colleagues too, so that we hear this evidence before the other counts because we have many points in common, before we start with the individual -- other counts because this is how the indictment is composed. Count 1 relating to all and the acts of the individual accused are not specified within that count.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So therefore there would be a list -- yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I do understand the reasoning behind this proposal, but I think we should -- there should be a special treatment for Mr. Papic charged under the first count, that is the count of persecution. We did actually start with Mr. Dragan Papic and then we studied the various geographical areas of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, our idea was, and you will say if it is good or not, but since the indictment contains, under Count 1, persecution, and it also charges all the accused with it and that on the counts of 2 then the crimes are specified as to the perpetrator. We thought we would call in five or ten witnesses who would speak on Count 1, that is persecution, and each one of us would then examine one or perhaps two or even perhaps three witnesses in relation to Count 1. When we complete this, then we shall proceed to individual acts pursuant to the indictment, colleague Radovic, colleague Slokovic-Glumac, and so on and so forth. That was the idea, and we thought that it might be acceptable to the Tribunal as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We appreciate this effort by Defence counsel to try to be economical. Yes, we can accept the idea that then you would produce a list, a joint list, as it were, of a certain number of witnesses who would be addressing only Count 1, but each witness should not be examined by various counsel, only, say, if I understood Counsel Pavkovic correctly, each counsel would examine two or three witnesses, so the same witness will be examined in chief only by one counsel. Then there would be cross-examination and -- yes, yes. On the other hand, the Prosecutor is right, we should -- I mean, then since Dragan Papic is only accused on Count 1, of course, Counsel Puliselic should play a major role, it is for you to decide, but this is also an area where Counsel Puliselic might wish to state his views. Then, after that we would move on to other counts, and we would then stick to the rules we decided, but we would not go back to Count 1. We would forget about Count 1. We would move on to other counts. Yes, Counsel Radovic and then Mr. Puliselic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I have a practical question. We shall submit to the Court the names and all the other particulars of our witnesses; however, there are also secret indictments, we shall need also protective measures for some of our witnesses. Should we apply for these immediately when compiling the list of witnesses, or when? Perhaps before we begin to examine the witnesses so as to avoid any problems if they refuse coming to The Hague unless they are issued guarantees, and only after they are issued guarantees. So when should we apply for the protective measures of free entry and free return?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: There are various means of handling this matter. The Court may issue safe conducts, or we can resort to a video link so they can be examined and cross-examined while staying in their place without coming here. Now, you should then ask the Court as soon as possible for protective measures, and then we will decide on those protective measures. One of the protective measures being also that we issue safe conduct, if need be.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what would suit us best to begin with. Of course, examining one in the courtroom is the best way, and besides, I am not really a particular supporter of all these modern gadgets that are applied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We agree with you, Counsel Radovic, not because we hate modern technology, but I agree on the substance, namely, that it is much better to have the witness here in court instead of in a far away place. All right. So you can ask for protective measures as soon as possible. You will file your request with the registry, and then we will decide on the matter in due time. Going back to the witnesses. Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, just one thing. You said that our learned friend Puliselic might have to say something, but as regards this general part, rather, the context or the persecution, Count 1, we think that the order in which the witnesses should be called should be a matter to be decided by the Defence, and we thought that, as we had said, each one of us would examine one witness and then, at the end of that general part, if Mr. Puliselic has only one count, that is his client has, then perhaps he should be the one to follow immediately after the general part with his list of witnesses so as to complete completely with Count 1 and then to proceed with those specific charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. We think it's a judicious and sensible suggestion, so we then will start with Count 1, with this pool of witnesses as it were, and then we will move on to Counsel Puliselic, his list of witnesses, and then we start with Counsel Radovic and Slokovic-Glumac. So, in a way, we are changing our proposals, but I think you are right, it's more appropriate. I wonder whether the Prosecution has any suggestion? Would you feel that it's appropriate? Any other matter? All right. So we can adjourn now. Yes, Counsel Krajina, sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I have a question, if I may, Mr. President, to hear what the Chamber thinks about it, and I'm referring to physical evidence, notably the documentation such as various certificates, decrees, rulings for one's ability to serve the army or whatever, or some certificates of political organisations, whether accused were members or not, passports so when the frontiers were crossed on various days and so forth, and I'm asking when will these documents be authenticated? Because if the Chamber decides that these documents need to be verified, then the witnesses should know that and we should know that we also have not only to call in the witnesses but people who would be verifying or authenticating those documents, that is if we're talking about seals and stamps in passports, we would be duty-bound to bring the person who stamped those passports to confirm that this was done. If it is a particular medical certificate, then we should evidently call in the doctor who did this or that to avoid that at the time, when a particular piece of evidence is being addressed, that we only then have to look for such witnesses which would only, of course, prolong the whole procedure. That was my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I will ask the Prosecution to state their views. I think probably the best way to go about this matter is to try to give the Prosecution, as soon as possible, the relevant documents, and then if they don't challenge the authenticity of those documents, there will be no problem, as it happened with the document produced by Counsel Pavkovic about this telephone -- I think it was Counsel Pavkovic -- the telephone list and so on, so we ask the Prosecution to tell us whether they were contesting the authenticity of this document. There was no challenge. So it's been admitted into evidence. So to save time, I would urge you, as I say, to turn over to the Prosecution as soon as possible the various exhibits you would like to produce so that they have enough time to verify the authenticity of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Lordship. We have submitted a major part of these documents to the Prosecution already and have done this long ago, but if there are still some which we have not submitted, handed over to the Prosecution, we shall do that. But, of course, we have already handed over most of the documents which have to do with our future witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Susak and then Counsel Slokovic-Glumac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Your Lordship, I only have one question. The Prosecution was planning to call in some witnesses and then decided not to, and the Defence meets with tremendous difficulties when it tries to find those witnesses, so I wanted to hear what have you decided. To call in those witnesses as witnesses for the Court or I have already heard of some cases where I shall evidently have to resort to that particular method, that is, I will meet with serious difficulties when trying to find some witnesses who were scheduled as witnesses for the Prosecution and the Prosecution simply decided not to call them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You may remember that Counsel Krajina has already submitted an application to the effect that we should call four, now three witnesses as Court witnesses, and we did comply with this request. You may wish to submit an application to this effect, and we will decide. We will, first of all, hear from the Prosecution, and then we will decide. This would be Prosecution witnesses who have not been called by the Prosecution and that you would --

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: In this particular case, they will become witnesses for the Defence -- no, rather, Court witnesses because we simply have no access to them, and I should like to have the Court, the Chamber, call them in as witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, but could you, as I say, submit an application giving reasons why you think they must be called by the Court in the interests of justice? I assume they are Muslims, so it's more difficult for you to call them, but, in addition to that, I wonder whether you could supply the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And they are in different towns and some other reasons too. Thank you very much, Your Lordship. I merely wanted to confirm what I already knew about Mr. Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: There is just one more thing. We have already tried to adduce some evidence or tender some documents, proposing to admit them as evidence, and this refers to documents which were already used in the Blaskic case, that is, most of these documents have been confirmed by witnesses and have been authenticated by various witnesses in the Blaskic case and we shall also be needing them in this particular case. We do not know if we have again to have each individual document authenticated once again, when they were authenticated by individual witnesses in the Blaskic case, would also apply to this Chamber. That is, may we tender in evidence some evidence, some certificates, which were admitted and authenticated by another Chamber in another case? Do we have to repeat the whole procedure? Do we have to bring in a witness every time we need the authentication and for the purposes of cross-examination and so forth? We shall be needing quite a number of documents from that particular case, so we should like to know what is your view on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes. On this matter, which is of great importance, and it will be quite frequent since the massacre in Ahmici is one of the main elements that is discussed as far as the criminal responsibility of General Blaskic is concerned, during these proceedings I mentioned a decision that was made by General Blaskic and his counsel as far as the massacre in Ahmici was concerned. So maybe there were a number of statements that were mentioned during the Blaskic case. However, I think we should remain as free as possible and the Judges should remain as free as possible in order to assess the value of one statement or one document in this case in particular. I think there is no direct communication between the Blaskic case and this particular case; however, I am not against it. We can use in this Defence case documents or testimonies -- of course, the Judges will decide which procedure we will have to follow -- but we could use testimonies and documents used in the Blaskic case. For instance, let me talk about the documents and their authenticity. One thing is to contest or admit the authenticity of one document; another thing is to give meaning, a particular meaning or weight to a document or a testimony. I'm referring particularly about death certificates. It is one thing to prove that a death certificate was issued by the competent authority and another thing to assess or to affirm that this document is saying the truth. If we consider that the authenticity of a document has been admitted in the Blaskic case, then it could be admitted in this case; however, the parties should -- and the Judges -- should remain free to give a specific meaning and a specific weight to this evidence. However, I think that it would be useful for you to adopt a very specific attitude on this question because I think this question will become more and more frequent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Of course, we are not bound by any determination or evaluation made by another Trial Chamber. It is for us to decide. But, in practical terms, anytime a document is produced in Blaskic is also produced here by Defence counsel, it should be turned over to the Prosecution. If the Prosecution does not contest the authenticity of that document, we would admit it into evidence, whatever the decision by the other Trial Chamber. As for the testimonies, of course, made in Blaskic, we can accept only those testimonies of witnesses who come here to testify in court because, I mean, as such, the transcript is of no great value. So therefore, as I say, I would urge the Defence to turn over to the Prosecution, as soon as possible, all those documents which have already been tendered in the Blaskic case so that we can speedily go about this matter whenever they are produced here for our case. Yes. Also, when the Prosecution receives those documents, it should try to decide on this matter as soon as possible and tell the Defence so the Defence may decide whether or not to call witnesses. Again, in the interests of an expeditious pace of our proceedings, it is better to -- I see the point made by the Defence counsel. If the authenticity is not contested by the Prosecution, of course, you don't need to call witnesses to authenticate those documents. All right. Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. President. A few moments ago, you said that you would welcome suggestions as far as the sites to visit are concerned during your visit in Ahmici. Would you like to hear the suggestions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Are we finished with all the questions related to the Defence case, the second phase of the Defence case, so to speak? No matters? Defence counsel don't want to raise any -- all right. So we close then the pre-Defence conference under Rule 73 ter and we quickly move on to our on-site visit. Yes. I understand some Defence counsel insisted that we should go from point 6 -- have you got the annex? This one? Annex 2. First of all, I was expecting -- before we take up this matter of where to go -- I was hoping to receive requests from the parties about the points on the itinerary from where they would like to make observations relating to this Defence case so that it's not done on the spot. We should know in advance at what particular point a particular Defence counsel or the Prosecutor would like to raise an issue. You know now the setting and the purpose of this visit. It's not an informal visit. It is something very formal and it is a judicial sitting, in a way. Elsewhere, but by the Court with the parties. You could maybe put in requests by tomorrow -- what about by 10.00? If you have any particular requests concerning points where you would like the Court to make particular observations? We know, for instance, about the request put in by Counsel Krajina about the visibility and so on. We will there decide what to do about your particular request, the visibility from the house of Vlatko Kupreskic up to the area of the woods. Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: No, I have no other questions or suggestions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I was told that -- I understand Counsel Slokovic-Glumac insists that we should try to walk from point 6 to yellow line, through a wood. Is there a path?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there is a footpath there from point 6 to the houses at Kupreskici. It leads through the forest. It's not a forest, in fact. There are a few trees and there is no problem going along, walking along the path. People live there. It is passable and quite clear. It is marked as a forest, as a wood, but there are few trees there. It would be essential to go on that -- along that path. We had agreed to walk through this area, but it has been omitted in this proposal. But this part is very important, this area is important for us. This is part of our defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We will ask -- because, you know, this plan has been approved by SFOR. We need to ask SFOR whether they give the okay about this short walk from 6 to M, to the group of houses, J, M, D -- all right. We can put it off.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: If that is not possible, then we could -- we should approach it from point 6 so that we see this valley from point 6, to approach it as close as possible. This is a small valley with a few trees. We will propose this in writing. We wrote it in our first proposal. We are repeating this request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. No other outstanding matter concerning the on-site visit? Anyway, if you have any suggestions or requests, could you please put them in by tomorrow at 10.00 so that we may consider them before we leave on Monday? All right. We can adjourn now. Yes, Counsel Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Very briefly. If I understood you correctly, our proposal, you spoke about it; you said you would decide about it. I don't have to repeat it tomorrow. You will decide on the spot about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. We will adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 5.50 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 30th day of November, 1998, at 9.30 a.m.
